title: Dynamical low-rank methods for the Wigner equation I: separable difference potential
abstract: Recent advances in dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) have demonstrated its effectiveness in high-dimensional simulations. However, existing DLRA algorithms still face significant challenges when handling systems that involve complex collision terms, including the pseudo-differential operator (${\rm Ψ}$) in the Wigner equation, a representative operator characterized by nonlocality. It is deserving to carry out a series of works to develop the DLRA algorithms for solving the Wigner equation. As the first step in this series of works, we propose an efficient DLRA algorithm for the Wigner equation, using a separable decomposition of the difference potential. We combine this separable assumption with two often-used truncations of ${\rm Ψ}$, namely $\mathcal{K}$-truncation and $\mathcal{Y}$-truncation, to obtain a kind of separated representation of ${\rm Ψ}$. Complexity analysis and several challenging experiments, including harmonic oscillators, Gaussian barrier scattering, electron-electron scattering, and a Helium-like system, all of which satisfy the separable assumption, confirm that the proposed DLRA algorithm has significant advantages, achieving a reduction in computational effort by one to two orders of magnitude in both runtime and memory requirements compared to the full-grid approach. It is worth noting that, even in the absence of a predetermined low-rank structure for the solution, DLRA can still serve as a numerical scheme that balances efficiency and accuracy.
summary: The paper introduces and validates a Dynamical Low-Rank Approximation (DLRA) method to solve the Wigner equation for various quantum systems. By exploiting a separable approximation of the potential, it transforms the computationally prohibitive nonlocal operator into a manageable low-rank form. This results in massive reductions in computational cost while maintaining high accuracy across diverse physical models.
main_problem: Developing an efficient Dynamical Low-Rank Approximation (DLRA) algorithm to solve the Wigner equation, which is complicated by its nonlocal pseudo-differential operator ($\Psi$DO).
main_result: The proposed DLRA method achieves a significant computational advantage, reducing runtime and memory requirements by one to two orders of magnitude compared to full-grid approaches across various quantum scattering systems.
method: The core technique involves applying the low-rank approximation (DLRA) to the Wigner function evolution, enabled by assuming a separable decomposition for the difference potential within the $\Psi$DO.
model_or_system: The study focuses on solving the Wigner equation, which describes the phase-space dynamics of quantum systems. Benchmarks include harmonic oscillators, Gaussian barrier scattering, electron-electron scattering (Fermion systems), and Helium-like atoms.
key_observables: Reduced Wigner function ($W(x, k, t)$) evolution, $L_2$ error ($\varepsilon_2$), and $\Psi$DO components ($Z_j, S_{ij}, L_i$).
important_parameters: Time step ($\Delta t$) convergence order (observed second-order), approximation rank ($r$), and the separability rank ($R$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the difference potential $D_V(x, y)$ can be approximated by a separable form, allowing the $\Psi$DO to be separated into manageable low-rank components.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate convergence analysis (error vs. rank/time step) for harmonic oscillators and Gaussian barriers, and show time evolution snapshots of reduced Wigner functions for electron-electron scattering and Helium-like systems.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, proposes the DLRA method utilizing separable decomposition of the potential, details the implementation via a projector-splitting integrator (Z $	o$ S $	o$ L steps), presents convergence analysis across multiple physical tests, and concludes with computational cost comparisons.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, scalable numerical framework for simulating quantum dynamics in phase space that bypasses the curse of dimensionality inherent in full-grid methods, which is crucial for studying complex many-body interactions.
